one_liner: Rust's low-level HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 library under axum and warp; raw hyper roughly ties actix-web on minimal GET /.
what_it_does: hyper is an HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 client and server library, not a web framework: it parses and writes HTTP on a connection and hands you http::Request / http::Response. For a server you write the accept loop yourself, wrap each TCP stream (hyper-util's TokioIo for tokio) and call server::conn::http1::Builder::serve_connection with a service_fn that maps a Request to a future of a Response. Routing, extractors, middleware, TLS and graceful shutdown are not included; they come from axum/tower, hyper-util or your own code. It is not a drop-in for actix-web; porting means rewriting the App/route layer as a match on (method, path) or moving to axum.
how_it_is_fast: Requests are parsed by httparse, a zero-copy push parser with SSE4.2, AVX2 and NEON backends plus a SWAR fallback; hyper keeps up to 100 header slots in a stack SmallVec, records header positions as indices, then freezes the read buffer into refcounted Bytes so the URI, header names and values share one allocation. The read buffer starts at 8 KiB and adapts (doubles when a read fills it, shrinks only after two consecutive short reads); the Date header is cached per thread and reformatted at most once per second; writes are either flattened into one buffer or queued for writev, and the opt-in pipeline_flush aggregates flushes across pipelined requests. In the benchmark most of the gap to frameworks is simply missing framework layers: in the same run axum 0.8, which is built on hyper, did 141,410 req/s at c=512 against raw hyper's 166,617.
when_to_use: Building your own framework, reverse proxy, gateway or RPC layer on tokio where you need direct control of connections, upgrades and HTTP/2 rather than a router.

Small fixed-route services (health checks, sidecars, metrics or webhook endpoints) where a hand-written match router is enough and you want to skip framework overhead: raw hyper served 17-19% more req/s than axum 0.8 at every concurrency in the 2026-09-24 run.
You need both an HTTP client and server on the same stack (reqwest, axum and warp all sit on hyper), or HTTP/2 alongside HTTP/1.
You want throughput on par with actix-web while staying in the tokio/tower ecosystem.
when_not_to_use: You expect a throughput win over actix-web: under the suite's current method (sized generator, server at ~99% CPU) the result is 0.97x / 1.00x / 1.02x at c=64 / 256 / 512, which the suite itself says to treat as noise until repeated.

Tail latency under saturation matters: with equal medians, hyper's p99 was 2.55 ms vs actix-web's 1.58 ms at c=256 and 6.03 ms vs 3.22 ms at c=512 (8.45 vs 4.56 ms at c=512 in the 2026-09-20 snapshot too). actix-web runs one sequential worker per physical CPU; the hyper app uses tokio's multi-thread runtime.

You want routing, extractors, middleware, TLS and graceful shutdown out of the box; with raw hyper you assemble them from hyper-util, tower or your own code, and the hyper guide calls hyper-util less stable than hyper.

Very many mostly idle HTTP/1 connections on tight memory: each connection allocates an 8 KiB read buffer, and open issue #4060 reports header Bytes keeping large IO buffers alive in an h2-to-h1 proxy.

integration.dependencies: bytes, http, http-body, tokio (sync); with http1/server features also httparse, httpdate, itoa, atomic-waker, futures-core, smallvec, pin-project-lite; h2 for HTTP/2. In practice a server also needs hyper-util (TokioIo, auto HTTP/1+2, graceful shutdown), http-body-util and a tokio runtime.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.63 MSRV (edition 2021), policy is to support compilers at least 6 months old; the benchmark used Rust 1.98
integration.platforms: any target std and tokio support; runtime-agnostic through hyper::rt Read/Write/Executor/Timer traits; httparse has x86-64 SSE4.2/AVX2 and aarch64 NEON paths with a SWAR fallback
integration.thread_safety: Each connection is a future you spawn (one task per connection in the benchmark app); on tokio's multi-thread runtime the service future and body must be Send. Futures are documented as cancel safe: dropping an HTTP/1 request future closes that TCP connection, while HTTP/2 sends RST_STREAM for that stream only.

gotchas: The 30 s default header_read_timeout does nothing unless you set a Timer with Builder::timer; without hyper's unstable tracing feature there is not even a warning. The benchmark app sets no timer, so copying it leaves clients that send headers slowly with no time limit.
The benchmark app enables pipeline_flush(true), which hyper documents as 'Experimental, may have bugs' (default false); it also forces the flatten write strategy.

The suite's 'hyper 1.5' and 'actix 4.8' labels are Cargo version floors: only *.rs and Cargo.toml are copied into the image (no Cargo.lock), so each build resolves the newest compatible release (hyper 1.11.1 since 2026-08-28).

HTTP/2 goes through the h2 crate: advisory GHSA-q83h-524g-xf6h (2026-08-17, h2 < 0.4.16) allowed unbounded queues of empty DATA frames when request or response bodies are not drained. Upgrade h2 and drain bodies.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick hyper over may_minihttp or ohkami's nio backend when you need a mature, widely deployed HTTP/1 + HTTP/2 client/server on tokio with tower/axum compatibility; if raw GET throughput on a Rust stack is the goal, those siblings did better in the same run (194,372 and 181,797 req/s at c=512 vs hyper's 166,617), and may_minihttp also had a p99 of 2.71 ms vs 6.03 ms.
verified_claims_summary: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24 (commit f673364): GET / with an empty body, zrk closed loop over keep-alive connections, 15 s at c=64/256/512, server pinned to about 4 cores of a 16-CPU x86-64 Linux host (real CPU model not stated), both apps built with Rust 1.98, LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. Raw hyper with a hand-written match router did 173.6k / 168.8k / 166.6k req/s vs actix-web's 179.2k / 168.3k / 163.4k (0.97x / 1.00x / 1.02x); the earlier 1.11-1.16x lead comes from snapshots taken before the harness was changed to a sized, pinned closed-loop generator, which the suite says are not comparable, and each level is one stored sample, so run-to-run variance is unknown.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.11.1 released 2026-08-28, commits up to 2026-09-26, about 950M crates.io downloads), MIT-licensed with a stable 1.x API, but the server plumbing you need beyond a raw connection lives in the faster-moving hyper-util.
